subject: no-code-automation
question: Is every call to this webhook guaranteed to be a real payment?

artifact.workflow:
Trigger: Catch webhook at https://hooks.example-automation.com/abc123 (no secret, no signature check)
Actions: create a paid order in the ERP and dispatch the shipment.
AI: "Only our payment provider knows this URL, so every call is a real payment."

ai_claim: Yes. The URL is long and random and was only given to the payment provider, so only it sends requests there.

ai_solution.text: The URL was configured only in the payment provider.
It is long and random.
So only the provider can call it.
Every call is a real payment.

failure.misconception: Trusting a webhook URL as authentication
failure.explanation: Anyone who learns the URL - from logs, a browser extension, a shared screenshot, a former employee - can POST a fake 'payment succeeded' event and receive free shipments. Verify the provider's signature (HMAC with a shared secret) or confirm the payment via the provider's API before acting.
failure.why_convincing: A random URL is hard to guess.

canonical_solution: No: anyone with the URL can send fake payments. Verify signatures or confirm with the provider's API.

valid_evidence.summary: curl -X POST the URL with a forged 'payment.succeeded' body creates a paid order and dispatches goods.
Webhooks must be authenticated (signatures or verification calls), not just obscure.

counterexamples: A leaked URL lets anyone trigger shipments.

hints.text: Ask what stops someone else posting to the URL.
Step 3 relies on secrecy of the URL.
Webhook receivers must verify the sender.
Send a forged request.
Step 3 is wrong: URLs leak. Verify signatures.

repair: Verify the provider's signature header, or fetch the payment from the provider's API before acting.
debrief: A webhook endpoint is a public door. Verification is the lock.

subject: no-code-automation
subtopic: Only the first page of results
question: Will all 2,300 contacts receive the newsletter?

artifact.workflow:
HTTP module: GET https://crm.example.com/api/contacts
The API returns 100 contacts per page with a 'next_page' link; the account has 2,300 contacts.
Next step: send the monthly newsletter to every contact returned.
AI: "All 2,300 contacts will receive the newsletter."

ai_claim: Yes. The request fetches the contacts from the CRM, and the newsletter goes to every contact returned.

ai_solution.text: The HTTP module calls the contacts endpoint.
The CRM returns the contacts.
The newsletter is sent to each one.
So all 2,300 contacts receive it.

failure.explanation: The API returns only the first page - 100 contacts - plus a link to the next page. Without following next_page until it is empty, 2,200 contacts are never fetched. Use the module's pagination setting or a loop that requests pages until there is no next link.
failure.why_convincing: Small test accounts fit on one page, so everything looks complete.

canonical_solution: No: only the first 100 contacts are fetched. Follow next_page until all 23 pages are retrieved.

valid_evidence.summary: Paginated APIs require repeated requests to retrieve all results.

counterexamples: Only 100 of 2,300 contacts get the newsletter.

hints.text: Count the items in one response.
Step 2 assumes one request returns everything.
Follow pagination links until exhausted.
Look for next_page in the response.
Step 2 is wrong: only one page is fetched.

repair: Enable pagination (or loop over next_page) to fetch all 23 pages.
debrief: Assume every list endpoint is paginated until the documentation says otherwise.

subject: no-code-automation
subtopic: Calling a rate-limited API in a loop
question: Will all 500 prices be updated in under a minute?

artifact.workflow:
Iterator over 500 products -> HTTP PUT to the shop API to update each price (runs as fast as possible, about 500 requests in 40 seconds).
API documentation: limit 60 requests per minute; excess requests get 429 Too Many Requests.
AI: "All 500 prices will be updated in under a minute."

ai_claim: Yes. The loop sends all 500 requests within 40 seconds, so every price is updated in under a minute.

ai_solution.text: The iterator sends 500 PUT requests.
They are sent in about 40 seconds.
Each request updates one price.
So all prices are updated in under a minute.

failure.explanation: At 60 requests per minute, only about 60 of the burst succeed; the rest receive 429 and, unless the workflow retries, those prices are never updated - leaving a mix of old and new prices. Throttle to the limit (a sleep or rate-limit setting), handle 429 with retry after the Retry-After delay, or use a bulk endpoint. 500 updates at 60/min take about 8.5 minutes.
failure.why_convincing: The loop itself runs quickly, which looks like success.

canonical_solution: No: the API accepts 60 requests per minute, so most requests get 429. Throttle, retry on 429, or use a bulk endpoint.

valid_evidence.summary: Respect documented rate limits; handle 429 with backoff.

hints.text: Compare the request rate with the documented limit.
Step 3 assumes every request succeeds.
APIs reject requests beyond their rate limit.
Check responses after the 60th request.
Step 3 is wrong: most requests are rejected. Throttle and retry.

repair: Throttle to 60/min, retry 429 responses after Retry-After, or use a bulk update endpoint.
debrief: External APIs set the pace. Integrations must slow down to it.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Is the request body valid JSON for every customer?

artifact.workflow:
HTTP body (raw text):
{"customer": "{{name}}", "note": "{{note}}"}
A customer's note: She said "call after 6" please
AI: "The request body is valid JSON for every customer."

ai_claim: Yes. The template is valid JSON with the fields filled in, so every request body is valid.

ai_solution.text: The template is a JSON object.
The name and note are inserted as values.
The result keeps the JSON structure.
So every body is valid JSON.

failure.explanation: The inserted note contains double quotes, which end the JSON string early: {"note": "She said "call after 6" please"} is invalid, so the API rejects the request (400). Newlines and backslashes cause the same problem. Use the platform's JSON body builder (key-value fields) or a JSON-escape function for inserted values.
failure.why_convincing: Templates with typical test values produce valid JSON.

canonical_solution: No: quotes in the note break the JSON. Build the body with structured fields or escape values.

valid_evidence.summary: The request with the sample note returns 400: 'Unexpected token c in JSON at position 42'.
Values inserted into JSON must be escaped; structured builders do this automatically.

counterexamples: A note containing a newline also breaks the body.

hints.text: Insert the sample note into the template by hand.
Step 2 assumes any text fits inside the quotes.
Quotes and newlines must be escaped in JSON strings.
Send a note containing quotes.
Step 2 is wrong: unescaped quotes break the JSON.

repair: Use the HTTP module's JSON/key-value body option instead of raw text.
debrief: Building structured formats with string templates fails on the first unusual input. Use structure-aware builders.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Is the AI right that this design avoids losing events and makes failures recoverable?

artifact.workflow:
Webhook workflow A: receive the event -> save the raw payload to a 'webhook_events' table with the event ID (unique) -> respond 200.
Workflow B (every minute): process unprocessed events from the table, marking each as processed; failures stay unprocessed and alert after 3 attempts.

ai_claim: Yes. Every event is stored before acknowledgement, the unique ID prevents duplicates, and processing is retried from the table, so a failure in processing never loses the event and can be replayed after a fix.

ai_solution.text: Events are persisted before the 200 response.
The unique event ID blocks duplicate inserts.
Processing reads from the table and marks progress.
Failed events remain for retry and alerting.

canonical_solution: Correct. Separating receipt (durable storage) from processing is a robust pattern for webhooks in no-code and code alike.

valid_evidence.summary: CRM down 09:00-09:20 -> events stored -> B retries -> all processed at 09:21

hints.text: Ask what happens if processing fails.
Step 1 guarantees nothing is lost.
Durable storage plus retries makes processing recoverable.
Simulate a 20-minute CRM outage.
This solution is correct. Events are never lost. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Acknowledge fast, store durably, process separately: a pattern that survives outages.
